claim: The plaintiff claimed that the Law Society of Hong Kong acted in a manner that was inconsistent with his rights under art 10 of the Bill of Rights and art 39 of the Basic Law by requiring him to prosecute his complaint against solicitors before the Solicitors Disciplinary Tribunal, and sought reimbursement for his costs.
requested_remedy: The plaintiff claimed that the Law Society of Hong Kong acted in a manner that was inconsistent with his rights under art 10 of the Bill of Rights and art 39 of the Basic Law by requiring him to prosecute his complaint against solicitors before the Solicitors Disciplinary Tribunal, and sought reimbursement for his costs.
parties: Defendant: THE LAW SOCIETY OF HONG KONG (1st Respondent), THE SOLICITORS DISCIPLINARY TRIBUNAL (2nd Respondent)

facts.F1: The applicant, Philippe Frederic Delhaise, was involved in a divorce petition in 1988. An ex parte injunction was obtained by his then-wife through her solicitors against him, which was subsequently discharged due to material non-disclosure.
facts.F2: The applicant filed a complaint with the Law Society against the solicitors involved for misconduct in obtaining the ex parte injunction.
facts.F3: The Law Society, after a protracted investigation, decided not to submit the matter to the Tribunal Convenor of the Solicitors Disciplinary Tribunal Panel for further handling of the complaint.
facts.F4: The Chief Justice of the Court of Final Appeal submitted the matter to the Tribunal Convenor for disposal, which was followed by the Tribunal Convenor constituting a Solicitors Disciplinary Tribunal to inquire into and investigate the complaint.
facts.F5: The Council, however, decided that the Law Society should not take up the prosecution of the complaint before the Tribunal, obliging the applicant to appear in person before the Tribunal and prosecute his own complaint against the solicitors.
facts.F6: The Tribunal dismissed the disciplinary proceedings and ordered the applicant to pay the costs of the solicitors and the Tribunal.
facts.F7: The applicant appealed to the Court of Appeal, which dealt with preliminary matters in camera and held that the applicant had no right of appeal to the Court of Appeal. The Court also set aside the costs order made by the Tribunal against the applicant.
facts.F8: The applicant commenced the present proceedings on 7 December 2007, asking for leave to apply for judicial review of the Tribunal's refusal to reimburse him for his costs.
facts.F9: Article 10 of the Hong Kong Bill of Rights was not engaged in the present case because the proceedings before the Tribunal were not to determine the applicant's own rights and obligations.
facts.F10: The applicant was only a complainant or victim of the alleged misconduct of the solicitors and his role could not go beyond that of a complainant or a victim of the alleged misconduct.

reference_issues: Whether the Law Society of Hong Kong acted in a manner that was inconsistent with the applicant's rights under art 10 of the Bill of Rights and art 39 of the Basic Law by requiring him to prosecute his complaint against solicitors before the Solicitors Disciplinary Tribunal.
Whether the applicant was entitled to reimbursement for his costs incurred in prosecuting his complaint against the solicitors.

facts.F3: Her claim was made on the basis that, if refouled, she would be harmed or killed by her three creditors, named, Tuyet, Xuan and Thang.
facts.F4: According to the applicant, she borrowed loans from the three creditors in early 2014 to start her own trading business.
facts.F5: The loan agreements denoted that she would have to repay the loans within one year.
facts.F6: In middle to late 2014, her goods were confiscated two or three times and her business had suffered a significant loss.

facts.F10: There were two subsequent incidents in which Tuyet scolded and threatened her without harming her.
facts.F11: Xuan and Thang only made verbal threats through phones.
facts.F12: The time when they visited the applicant’s house posing death threats, the applicant was not home.
facts.F13: Feared that the creditors would materialize the threats, the applicant fled to Hong Kong for protection.
